segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What’s your name in English?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Jerry Ice.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Now in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Inol Unesdal.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Inol?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Inol.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What does that mean?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: I really don’t know. My uncle would say, “Come here, Inol.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you didn’t know what it meant?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: No, I didn’t.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Isn’t that what they call a badger?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I don’t know.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: There’s someone from the Eastern Band that has that name, Inol. They think it means badger. It could be what your name means.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Maybe so.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where were you born?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Briggs.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s where they caught you (born at home) they say?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You weren’t born at the hospital?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: No, Tahlequah – no, the hospital in Borger, Texas.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s where you were born?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How did you come to live here?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: My father worked for Phillips Petroleum. He got sick for a while and they took him off work. He had land allotments here. He had several of them and so we came here. I was about six years old.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you came here?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Then you grew up here?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many were there in your family?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Six.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were all of you Cherokee speakers?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: No. I was the only one.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Just you?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How did you become the only child to speak Cherokee in your family?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: My mother was in hospital at Talihina. I was with my dad all the time. He always spoke Cherokee. That’s how it started. The other kids were going to school and they only heard English.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did your mother get sick?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. She had tuberculosis.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long did she stay in the hospital?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: She went there twice. The first time she was there eight years. Then she got sick again and had to go back for... maybe four that time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She was in there a long time.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. Quite a while. Dad was working and I was always with him when he went. Always right behind him.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When your dad came back here, what kind of work did he do?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: He did anything. He was a handyman. He fixed fence posts, cut firewood, and then he started working at Tahlequah Lumber Company – Bob Cunningham’s business. He worked as a carpenter. He worked there a long time. Then he had a heart attack. The doctor said he shouldn’t be working. He was hardheaded and he worked anyway. He had a heart attack three times. Then he had to take it easy. He just worked everywhere.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Growing up, what did you all do?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: We had kind of like a farm. We grew corn, potatoes, and beans. We had four horses. They were workhorses, so we were always behind them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you ride them, too?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How did you store your harvest?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Some of it was canned. Tomatoes and beans. I forgot... and turnips.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: daqw(i)san(i).

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. My father would make a hole in the ground and cover it with straw. When it got real cold, about January, then we would go get some out.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about potatoes?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: About the same thing. As for the fruits, they dried them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They dried them?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: They dried those and some tomatoes. We would sell some, too. That’s how my father made some money.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: To help out with income?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What’s your parents’ names?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Ge hid, was my mother’s name. Last name was Hogner. My father’s name was Tsistetsi Unesdal.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was he related to that man that used to sing, Floyd?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What’s your wife’s name?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Katie.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long have you been married?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: It will be 20 years in January.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many children do you all have?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Along with a previous marriage there are five girls and one boy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They’re all grown up with children of their own?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you have grandchildren?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Oh there is quite a few.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: There's quite a few.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: 24 of them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you have great-grandchildren?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do any of them speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: No. One of them tries to speak it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do they all live close by?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes, but one of them lives in Florida.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Florida?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. You know Jerri Lynn, don’t you?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, that's where she's at. That’s the youngest, right?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. She went there a few years ago.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Does she come home for visits?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. She came back for a while in July. It’s hard to get a job around here.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: One of my grandchildren lives in Kansas. They can’t find a job around here. He’s been training horses since he was 13 years old and still doing that.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Oh, training horses.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes. Working with racehorses. Not racing them, but exercising them.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: I tried racing horses in Colorado a long time ago. I was 112 pounds. Then I got too heavy and I had to quit. [laughs]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes. That’s how it goes.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. That’s why they have skinny riders. [laughs]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I guess they’re feeding you good now?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. [laughs]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The first time I saw you, you were real small.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When we left Sycamore, what did you do for work?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: I was working on the pipeline in Texas. The last time, I was working in New York. Then I was preaching for a while.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you’re not doing that anymore?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Just a little, because I work, too. That’s the reason. I help Jess. Jess French at Eldon.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Are you a member there?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you go to school at?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: I went to Briggs in grade school. Then two years at Tahlequah. Then I got my GED.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you didn’t graduate from high school?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: No, I didn’t.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you were going to Briggs, what did they think about you? Did you speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did they think about you speaking Cherokee?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Most of the kids spoke it. The principal spoke Cherokee, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He spoke Cherokee?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Who was the principal?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Lloyd Baker.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was he white?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And he spoke Cherokee?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. He was white but he spoke good Cherokee. He spoke good Cherokee – he just had a white face.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did your family, such as your aunts and uncles, live close by?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes, one of them lived in Stilwell, named Kenny. Another lived in Muskogee. My grandmother was everywhere.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They moved around a lot?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about when you lived in Colorado, can you tell us about that?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: It was dry there. We worked with broom corn, seeding it and all. We worked a little over six months there and then we came back here. I went with Coleman McLemore.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: To broom corn?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. To work with broom corn.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did you do with the broom corn? What did you cut down?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: It’s like corn. It’s tall and you cut it down. They saddle and break down. They make saddles and bundles. They would make brooms out of the straw, part of it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They did make brooms out of it, didn’t they?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes, they did.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you just cut the tops off and not the bottom?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. We cut the bottoms, and the tops was used for brooms. The stalks were ground up for cattle feed.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, that makes sense. About five years ago, they ran out of hay back home and he fed them corn stalks and the cows ate it.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How much did they pay?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: $10 a day.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: For one day. Was it hard work?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. It took about an hour to do one row. We had five to start with. We would cut all of them. You had to start in the middle and when you finished, he would say to make sure you cut them all. I said OK. I would just cut here and then cut over there. Someone asked me what I was doing. I told him I was cutting stalks. He said, “You’re supposed to cut one row before you start another.” I was just cutting everywhere and I was slow. About noon I was finally finished with one row. They were laughing at me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you were supposed to finish five rows?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: A day?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. Some of the fast ones would do maybe 10 or 12 rows a day.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they get paid more?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They were fast workers.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. They could cut fast and probably do up to 15 rows.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they just leave them there after they cut them?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: No. They would make saddles out of them. After we cut down the stalks, they would bundle them up. They would bring trailers and they would put them in there then they would take them and put them in a grinder. It sure made a lot of dust and sometimes it was hard to breathe. Some of the older ones wore bandanas all the time. I wondered why and that was the reason.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Because it was dusty.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. In the morning, it was kind of warm. The older ones brought coats, and I wondered why because it was warm. Then I found out why. About four o’clock that afternoon, there was a black cloud in the west. About four thirty, a dust storm started. It was so dusty and it got really cold. It changed real quick. I didn’t have a coat and one of the older men came over and handed me a coat. I was so thankful. Then we went back to camp. There was a 16-penny nail holding the bed up by an inch and a half.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, they had a place for you all to sleep?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes, and they fed us morning, noon, and evening.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was the person’s name that you was working for?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Rand Rogers.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: My father used to go. I don’t remember who he worked for, but they used to ride the bus.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: We went by car. Me and Sampson McCarter. They paid him $10 a person for taking them. He would drop me off, then there was some that came back home. He would go there in a day then head back that evening.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many of you were there working?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: About 30.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many acres of broom corn were there?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: One of them, Rand’s, was 280 acres.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I would never finish with that much acreage.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: It was about November when they got done with it. Then they would make shocks. Bundle them up for cattle feed. It would be cold and snowing at times. The first time we went there, about December 23rd, my father said, “Let’s go. It’s going to snow soon.” I asked him if he really thought so and he said yes. We left from there and it started snowing at about Boise City. When we got to Campo, there was about two and a half feet of snow. We barely made it out of there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s where my father used to go, Campo.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Campo?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: I also went to Walsh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes, he went there, too, sometimes. Did you ever go to the mountains?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You’ve never been there?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: My boy that lives in Kansas used to live in Colorado at one time. He wanted to take me to the mountains and I said, “No, let’s just stay down here where we’re at.”

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: That’s what Wayne Pinkerton did on one of his mission trips. I can’t remember where at in the mountains, but he said he was barely breathing up there. He wanted someone to send him some oxygen.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is there anything that you would like to talk about specifically? Sometimes people want to talk about a certain thing. We can make time for that now.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Well one time D.J. Smith and I went to Jay. We left from there about 12 o’clock at night. On Highway 10, we pulled over by the graveyard called Molly Fields Cemetery. There was a ball of light that was bluish in color and it would go up and down. It went north then it would go south then right down to the ground. It did this several times. I was scared so I got back in the car. I started the car, then D.J. ran back and got in and asked me what that was. I said, “I don’t know. I think it was a ghost.” That was something else! He kept asking me what I thought and I kept telling him, “I don’t know.” When we got back home, I told my father and he said it was a new grave there and that glowing thing was caused from gases from the new body. A fox fire.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: A what?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: A fox fire.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Fox fire.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. As a body dries up, that’s what happens.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Huh.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: It was like a ghost.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I’ve seen one of those things.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Oh?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We were at Marble City and we were on our way home with our two children. We saw one about this big and tall. It was moving along about this high in the air. When the kids saw it then they were scared. It was there for quite a while, then it faded out eventually.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Hmm.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Then the other one was by Cave Springs School. We were coming home from work. Me and my boss. We saw one rolling around and it was a bright fire. For a while we thought there was a train going by. You know they cause sparks sometimes. It was by a field by the railroad tracks, but it wasn’t a train.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It was just rolling around. It sure was interesting!

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Sometimes it’s not what we think it is. One time we went to the creek and my father was ahead of everyone. When we got there, there were a lot of snakes there. I told him, “There are snakes!” But he went on. I stopped and there were all kinds of snakes in there. My father said it was mating season, that’s why. One time we went to a strawberry patch. I went to use the bathroom by the trees. There was a black snake there. Boy, that thing was biting every which way, and I never knew one of them to bite – that kind of snake anyway. It was snapping. I told my father about it. That snake was changing his skin and that skin had got over his eye. He couldn’t see so he was just biting at the sounds.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When it’s changing into winter, they go blind and anything that makes a noise they will try to bite it. That’s when they are dangerous.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes, same for the one they call copperhead.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Tso.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I have snake boots. I wear them when I go in the woods.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I’m scared of them.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: One time I went to my mother’s. There’s a trail that went to a spring and that’s where we got water. Boy, my mother let out a scream. She said, “Snake!” I asked what kind it was. “Boy,” she said. “A dangerous one.” “How big is it?” “It’s about four feet and was like a stove pipe.” I said, “Golly!” I’m thinking that it’s a rattlesnake. I went over there and I didn’t see anything. I asked her where it was and she said, “It’s right there.” She said, “Watch out! Watch out! It’s right there!” I looked and it was just a pine knot!

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And it scared her.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes, it scared her. She couldn’t see very well at the time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You said you used to preach some?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where were you preaching at?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Echota.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Echota?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were there Cherokees there?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. There were Cherokees that came. There were a few of them. Levi Handle and Jeanette and Ella May Foster. They were members for a while. There was someone else. What’s his name... Croley?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Croley Proctor?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Deacon.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: In your own way of thinking, with the way the Cherokee language is right now, what do you think is going to become of it?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: I think it may just be the end of it because they’re not learning it as far as the kids. That’s why this here school is really good because it’s all Cherokee. There’s one boy I remember and he only spoke English. He was about nine years old. He started trying to speak Cherokee. Now he speaks really good Cherokee. They also have the Cherokee Choir now. That’s the only way it’s going to stay and we keep it is if we teach them. If we don’t teach them, then we’re going to lose it. When I was in the military, boy I lost a lot of it. I was at Germany and I would talk to my father on the phone. We only spoke Cherokee. The operator was German and you could hear them clicking there wondering what we were talking about.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long was you in the military?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: It was 13 years.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What year was it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was there a war going on at that time?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. There was the Vietnam War.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you have to go out to fight?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was it like?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: It was bad. They were 13 years old. They would start training kids when they were 8 years old. Then at 13 they were full-fledged soldiers at that age and were sent out to fight. It was so dangerous for kids out there and carrying guns. There was a lot of cocaine being used there also. Those kids were out of their minds. There were women out there, too. They called them mama-sans. One time we were sent to a village for a search and seizure. The captain said, “That’s just an old mama-san. Leave her alone.” So, we went on and when we had gone past her, she got up and she had a machine gun. She killed about four soldiers in my platoon. So, you have to watch everything that’s there because of things like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, the women fought, too?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And you never knew when they would attack.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you saw people getting killed?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Huh?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you saw people getting killed?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes, I did. That’s why it was so hard for me when I came back home. It says in the Bible not to murder. That’s why it was so hard for me. Then there was an elder at Jay that told me that it’s like you had a job to do. You did what you had to do. It was the way it was supposed to be. He said it was survival. Survival of the fittest. I believe it was the reason I was sent there. I would rather fight them on their land than have them come on mine and me trying to push them back. I think that’s the reason. It’s a lot worse now. More sickness everywhere.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you kill anyone?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes, a few of them. One time, we finished inspecting a village and we heard a da, da, da, da! I was sitting back there – .30 caliber. I stood up. I could see some people walking around. So, I returned fire. I killed seven children.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: About what age were they?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: They had to be about six, nine, 12, maybe. That’s why I had a hard time with it. I had PTSD. I had it really bad. At night I could still see those children. I was afraid to sleep because I didn’t want to see that again. Sometimes I still see all that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You said there’s more sickness and disease in the world today. What do you think your grandchildren are going to see in the future?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Could be just anything nowadays. They will see sickness. They don’t really care anymore. They don’t really go to church that much anymore. They just try anything and they don’t think anything about it. Then there was Covid that came around, and I got sick with it once. Just me. That’s the reason I’m on hospice, on account of Covid in my lungs. I have a hard time breathing. I’ve been on hospice over a year now. Sometimes I can barely breathe. That’s the reason I use oxygen most of the time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do they still help you with that?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes, they still do. Most all the time. A nurse comes to my house and a doctor. A chaplain comes, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do your girls still come to see you?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. One of them lives at Jay. She came to visit about two weeks ago. That boy lives at Peggs.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How old is he?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is he the oldest?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I’ve never seen him before.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: He was in the military when he was 20. He barely made it back. He got blown out of a Humvee. One time he came to my house, and he wanted to go out in the woods, so we went. After a while he said, “Stop, stop. I’m just so tired. I can barely walk,” he said. He said, “That’s not right, Dad. I’m ailing. It shouldn’t be that you can out-walk me. I just can’t do it anymore.” When we got back to the house, he could hardly walk. His wife said, “What are you doing?” He told her he was having a hard time walking. Yesterday, my granddaughter-in-law passed away. She was 38.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What’s her name?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Felicia Ice.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She wasn’t a Cherokee speaker?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: No. Yesterday evening that boy was cleaning out his pistol and shot his hand. They took him to Tulsa and then they took him to Oklahoma City. I guess he did a good job on it because they said he was going to need quite a few surgeries. It’s hard to figure.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How old is he? Did you say 58? What’s his name?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Jerry.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Jerry.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Yes. They call him Cherokee. In Cherokee. But he uh, I guess he done a pretty good job on it because he’s going to have to have quite a few surgeries on it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We are finishing up now.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: OK.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: If there’s anything you would like to say or leave something to say for other people, what would it be?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: Such as what?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Anything you would like to say to the younger generation?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: I would just like to encourage them to try hard to learn to speak the Cherokee language, to try to speak it every day so that there will always be a Cherokee Nation. If they quit speaking Cherokee and only speak English, then there will be no Cherokee language. Those senators and congressmen. One thing the military had was code talkers. Creeks, Choctaws, Cherokees, all kinds. I know about that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Are we finished now?

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: I think that will be enough.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Alright. We appreciate you coming in.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: OK.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Take care of yourself.

segments.speaker: jerry-ice
segments.translation: OK, you too.
